interviewFlags.risks.earnedIncomeVaries.reason: Earned income is the largest source of payment errors, and wages that change month to month are the hardest to get right: a single pay stub doesn't show what a month of irregular hours or tips comes to.
probeQuestions: How many hours have you worked each week over the last month?
Do you get tips? About how much in a typical week?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors
NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

interviewFlags.risks.cashOrSelfEmploymen.reason: Cash, gig and self-employment income often isn't on the application at all, and isn't asked about unless someone asks specifically.
probeQuestions: Does anyone in the household do any work for cash, side jobs, or gig work?
About how much did that bring in over the last 30 days?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors
FRAC: A Backgrounder on SNAP Quality Control, Payment Error Rates, and Cost-Sharing

interviewFlags.risks.incomeChangedSinceP.reason: Income that's changed since the household on record — a job gained or lost, a raise, hours cut — is a leading cause of both overpayments and underpayments when it isn't reported. On a new application, that's since the application was filed.
probeQuestions: Has anyone started or stopped a job since your last renewal?
Has anyone's pay or hours changed?

sources.title: FRAC: A Backgrounder on SNAP Quality Control, Payment Error Rates, and Cost-Sharing
FNS SNAP Recertification Toolkit (June 2018)

interviewFlags.risks.householdChangedSin.reason: Who lives in the household and buys food together decides whose income counts. Changes are often unreported, and often not asked about at recertification.
probeQuestions: Has anyone moved in or out since your last renewal?
Does everyone who lives with you buy and prepare food together?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors
FNS SNAP Recertification Toolkit (June 2018)

interviewFlags.risks.shelterCostsCarried.reason: Shelter costs carried forward from the last certification without being asked about can be out of date in either direction: a move or a rent increase that's missed.
probeQuestions: Is your rent or mortgage still the same amount?
Have you moved since your last renewal?

sources.title: FNS SNAP Recertification Toolkit (June 2018)
NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

interviewFlags.risks.elderlyOrDisabledWi.reason: A member 60 or older, or disabled, may deduct medical costs. Missed deductions are among the most common fixable errors, and lead to underpayments.
probeQuestions: Does [member] pay for any doctor visits, prescriptions, or medical supplies?
About how much a month?

sources.title: NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates
FRAC: A Backgrounder on SNAP Quality Control, Payment Error Rates, and Cost-Sharing

interviewFlags.risks.childrenAndEarnersW.reason: Care for a child so a household member can work is deductible. When it's new it often isn't asked about, which leads to an underpayment.
probeQuestions: Does anyone look after the children while you work or go to school?
Do you pay for that care?

sources.title: NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

interviewFlags.risks.multipleProgramsApp.reason: Households on several programs face reporting rules that differ between them, which makes it harder to keep each program's information right.
probeQuestions: Have you reported this change to [other program] as well?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.incomeBel.reason: When reported income doesn't cover reported expenses, something the application doesn't show is paying the difference: unreported income, or help from outside the household. FNS-1104 makes it a probe.
probeQuestions: Your expenses are more than your income. How does the household make up the difference?
Does anyone help with bills — family, friends, or community organizations?

sources.title: FNS State SNAP Interview Toolkit (FNS-1104, revised June 2025)

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.wagesDiff.reason: Income an agency's data systems show but nobody confirms is an error the agency could have caught. A difference from the wage records needs explaining before it's resolved either way.
probeQuestions: The state's records show [amount] in wages for [member]. Does that sound right?
Did [member] have another job, or more hours, during that time?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors
NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.incomeDif.reason: A recorded amount that doesn't match its pay stubs usually means a pay frequency was converted wrongly — weekly, every two weeks, and twice a month are easy to confuse.
probeQuestions: How often is [member] paid — every week, every two weeks, or twice a month?

sources.title: NGA: SNAP Payment Accuracy — Strategies for Reducing Payment Error Rates

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.household.reason: The household's size decides its benefit. A size that doesn't match the members listed means someone is missing or counted who shouldn't be.
probeQuestions: Who lives with you and buys and prepares food with you?

sources.title: GAO-05-245: Food Stamp Program — States Have Made Progress Reducing Payment Errors

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.jobWithou.reason: A job with no income recorded is information that arrived but wasn't applied — the most common kind of agency error.
probeQuestions: Is [member] still working at [job]? How much are they paid?

sources.title: APHSA: Payment Error Rates — Understanding What They Are and How to Support SNAP Agencies in Reducing Them

interviewFlags.inconsistencies.earnedInc.reason: Earned income with no job behind it can't be verified or updated when the job changes, and is often a job that ended but wasn't closed out.
probeQuestions: Where does [member] work? Are they still working there?

sources.title: APHSA: Payment Error Rates — Understanding What They Are and How to Support SNAP Agencies in Reducing Them

oneof-discriminator.description: Inline oneOf with a discriminator property, where all variants are defined within the same file (not via external $ref). Exercises discriminated union rendering, discriminator label resolution, and variant expansion in the explorer.

anyof.description: anyOf composition — a field that may satisfy more than one schema simultaneously (e.g., a record with both electronic and manual verification on file). Exercises anyOf rendering and the semantic distinction from oneOf.

additional-properties-map.description: Map type using additionalProperties to allow arbitrary key-value pairs (e.g., labels or metadata). Exercises additionalProperties rendering in the explorer and map validation in the schema validator.

read-only-field.description: Field marked readOnly: true — server-generated and never accepted in write operations. Common for IDs, computed values, and lifecycle timestamps. Exercises readOnly rendering in the explorer and write-operation filtering.

deprecated-field.description: Field marked deprecated: true with a migration note pointing to its replacement. Exercises deprecated field rendering in the explorer and tooling warnings.

string-format.description: String field with a format constraint (uuid, date-time, date, email, etc.). Exercises format rendering in the explorer and format validation.

polymorphic-base.description: Base schema extended via allOf in Create and Update variants. The Create variant adds required fields; the Update variant applies minProperties: 1 for partial updates. Exercises allOf merging and the Create/Update schema pattern.

array-of-enum.description: Array of enum values. Exercises array-of-enum rendering in the explorer and array item validation in the schema validator.

x-enum-source.description: Enum values resolved at build time from an external source (e.g., a state machine's state IDs) via the x-enum-source extension, rather than hardcoded in the OpenAPI spec. Exercises the resolver's x-enum-source injection.

nullable-state-gated-field.description: Nullable field that is only present after a lifecycle transition (e.g., a timestamp set when an application is submitted). Exercises nullable field rendering and the pattern of state-gated fields.

nullable-conditional-field.description: Nullable field whose presence depends on another field's value (e.g., a benefit amount present only when eligible is true). Exercises nullable field handling and conditional presence patterns.

external-ref-shared-defs.description: External $ref to a shared $defs schema in a separate file. Exercises the resolver's cross-file $ref resolution and the explorer's external schema name rendering.

external-ref-defs-oneof.description: External $ref to a $defs schema that is itself a oneOf with a discriminator. Exercises: (1) cross-file $ref resolution, (2) discriminated union rendering with labeled variants, (3) field inventory handling of oneOf inside an external $defs ref.

allof-inline-required.description: allOf composition that adds inline required fields without duplicating properties (e.g., a Create variant that adds a required field to a base schema). Exercises the resolver's allOf merging and the explorer's allOf rendering.

paginated-list.description: Collection endpoint returning items/total/limit/offset/hasNext. The standard blueprint pagination envelope. Exercises paginated list rendering and parameter validation (limit, offset, sort, search).

sub-resource.description: Resource nested under a parent at a path like /parents/{id}/children. Full CRUD scoped to the parent. Exercises nested routing, parent FK validation, and sub-resource list/detail rendering in the explorer.

singleton-sub-resource.description: Single resource nested under a parent at a path like /parents/{id}/summary, with no item-level ID. Accessed only through the parent. Exercises singleton sub-resource routing and composition rendering.

intra-domain-fk.description: Intra-domain x-relationship foreign key linking a sub-resource back to its parent resource within the same domain. Exercises cross-reference rendering in the explorer and FK validation.

cross-domain-fk.description: Cross-domain x-relationship foreign key linking a resource in one domain to a resource in another. Exercises cross-domain reference rendering and FK validation across domain boundaries.

rpc-state-machine-action.description: RPC-style state machine action with a generated POST endpoint. Exercises the RPC overlay generator, x-relationship tagging, and state machine → API cross-linking in the explorer.

state-machine-guard.description: Named boolean condition (CEL expression) attached to a state machine action. The action can only be triggered when all guard conditions pass. Exercises guard evaluation, actor role checking, and guard composition (any/all).

state-machine-timer.description: Timer declaration on a state machine. The scheduling service emits a callback event ({domain}.{id}) when the timer fires; the machine subscribes to react. Exercises timer declaration rendering and the timer → event subscription link.

state-machine-subscription.description: State machine subscribing to a domain event emitted by a different domain. The handler runs steps (create, emit, call) automatically when the event arrives. Exercises cross-domain event subscription and handler rendering.

info.description: What the server does from the contracts alone, feature by feature. A household's SNAP application is the example throughout: it's created, read through compositions and edited through one, taken through its lifecycle, checked by rules, and traced in the event log.

workflows.description:
- A resource's contract declares what a client app may write and what the server keeps, and the server serves both.
- It also checks relationships between records, takes uploads, and searches, sorts and pages lists, from declarations alone.

steps.description:
Create an application

- The client app sent an `ApplicationCreate` and got back an `Application` — two schemas, not one. The contract declares the shape a client app may write separately from the shape the server keeps.
- `id`, `confirmationNumber`, `status`, `submittedAt`, `openedAt` are marked readOnly, so they are not on the shape the client app sent at all. The server filled them in because the contract says they exist.
- `programCount` is declared as a derived field, with the expression `this.programsAppliedFor.size()`. Nothing stores it: the server evaluates that expression every time the record is read.
- `channel` is an enum in the contract — online, phone, in_person, mail. A value outside that list is refused by the schema, and no validation was written for this endpoint to do it.
- `slaInfo` already has a running clock: the SLA contract says `snap_standard` assigns itself to every application for SNAP, runs 30 days, warns at 80% of it, and stops while `status` is withdrawn. The clock is a declaration, not a cron job somebody remembered to write.
- `201` and `400`, `422`, `500` are all declared on this operation, and the server worked out which one applied and returned it. None of them are canned.

Upload a document

- This body is `multipart/form-data`, not JSON. The contract declares `file` with format: binary, which is how an OpenAPI document says bytes, and `documentTypeId`, `title` alongside it as ordinary fields. One operation in the whole set sends something that is not JSON, and it is the one most mocks fall over on.
- What came back describes the upload and does not contain it. The bytes were hashed as they were read and then dropped — `contentHash` and `sizeBytes` are kept on the version this created, which `latestVersionId` names, and the file itself is nowhere. Nothing the server holds can leak something nobody meant to share.

file.content: Hashed on the way in, and then thrown away.

steps.description:
Attach a document that isn't there

- Refused with `422`. `proofOfIncomeDocumentId` declares `x-relationship` to document management's `Document`, so the server looked for that document and found none.
- The refusal names the field and the id, in the same shape as a schema error. The id is a valid uuid, so the schema had nothing to object to.
- The check crosses domains, from intake into document management, and nothing was written for it. Every field that declares a relationship is checked the same way, on every create and update.

Edit and attach the document

- A third shape: `ApplicationUpdate` is what the client app may send here, and it is not `Application` either.
- `proofOfIncomeDocumentId` is the id of the `Document` the client app uploaded a moment ago, and `links.proofOfIncomeDocument` is where to read it. The field declares an `x-relationship` to document management's `Document` with style: links-only, so the response keeps the id and adds a link to the record, and nothing builds that URL in the client app.
- `updatedAt` moved on its own. Everything the request did not mention is as it was.
- `id`, `confirmationNumber`, `status` are not on `ApplicationUpdate` at all, so there is no way to send them and nothing to reject.
- `200` and `400`, `404`, `422`, `500` are all declared on this operation, and the server worked out which one applied and returned it. None of them are canned.

List the applications

- `q`, `sort`, `limit` are in the request above, and `q`, `limit`, `offset`, `sort`, `status`, `channel` are all declared on the operation. Declaring them was the whole of the work — the searching, filtering and paging came with them.
- `x-sortable` lists `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `submittedAt`, `status`, `channel` as the fields that may be sorted, and -createdAt as the order when a request does not say. Any other field is refused by name. The allowlist is that declaration — there is no check written for this endpoint.
- `items`, `total`, `limit`, `offset` — the page envelope is the contract's shape, not a convention the server chose.

workflows.description: - A composite view puts several records together into one response, from a declaration in the contracts. A `view` is read at one endpoint; a `sectionView` is read section by section.

steps.description:
Read the application's summary

- `applicationSummary` is a `view`: the application's `programsAppliedFor`, `status` and `channel`, with its `members` alongside. Nothing stores this shape; the server assembles it from the records when the client app asks.
- Its fields choose what each part shows, so a summary carries only what a reader of a summary needs.

Build a view of the application

- Nothing stores this shape. The composition names `programsAppliedFor`, `status` and the server reads those fields off the stored application when the client app asks for it.
- It also pulls in `members`, which live in their own collection. Reading this without the composition means a request for the application and 1 more for the rest, then assembling them in the client app.
- This is where the `_links` on the application came from. `applicationSummary`, `applicationReview` set `parentLink`, so the server added `/summary`, `/review` to every application it returns. The application's own schema says nothing about either of them.

workflows.description:
- `applicationDetails` is an editable composition: the application and its members and incomes as one document, which a client app changes with a JSON Patch (RFC 6902).
- The composition is a wrapper. Each change in a patch is made through its record's own operation, on behalf of whoever sent the patch, so that operation's checks, permissions and events apply. A patch is kept whole or not at all.

steps.description:
Read the application's details

- The application is under `application`, with its members and incomes beside it, each keyed by its id. A patch names one record by that key, as in `/incomes/{incomeId}/amount`, so a path always names the same record however the list changes.
- Records come whole, each as its own read returns it.

Add a household in one patch

- Two members and an income, in one request. The client app chose each new record's id, so the income can name its member, Maria, before she exists.
- The server created Maria and Luis through `createApplicationMember` and the income through `createApplicationIncome`, Maria first, since the income names her.
- Each record sent its own created event, and each names this patch as its cause.

Change the income from 1100 to 1250, only if nobody else changed it first

- The patch starts with a test: it checks the amount is still 1100, the value the client app read, and changes nothing. If the amount is different, the whole patch is refused. The replace after it runs only if the test passed.
- The change went through `updateApplicationIncome`, with its checks and its updated event.

Send the same change again, as a client app that read the income before it changed

- Refused with `409`: the amount is 1250 now, so the test for 1100 fails. A client app working from an older copy can't overwrite a change it didn't see.
- Nothing in the patch was kept, not even the change after the failed test.

Send one bad change among good ones

- The patch adds a member, Ana, and clears the income's amount, which an income can't do without.
- Refused with `422`, naming the income's change. Ana was created first and then removed again: an undo log puts back what the earlier changes wrote, and the events they caused were held and never sent.

Read the application's details again

- The income is still 1250, and Ana isn't among the members.

Try to change what the state machine owns

- Refused with `422`. `status` is marked readOnly: the server sets it, and the application's state machine moves it through its actions. A patch can change only what the record's own update would let the client app change.

Retry the household patch with its key

- The same patch with the same `Idempotency-Key` gets the first answer back, marked `Idempotent-Replayed`. Maria and Luis aren't added twice.
- A client app that lost the first response can retry safely.

Remove a member

- One change removes Maria, through `deleteApplicationMember`. Her income goes with her: the income's `memberId` declares onDelete: cascade, as OData's OnDelete does.
- The patch didn't have to name the income. The data model says it belongs to her.

workflows.description: - An application's lifecycle is a state machine in the contracts. The server moves the record only along the transitions it declares, and runs each action's steps: setting fields, calling procedures, sending events.

steps.description:
Stand in for the scheduler

- Nothing in the contract set implements a scheduler, and `submit` asks for one 72 hours out. That gap is declared, not accidental.
- This registers a stand-in for `platform.timer.requested`, so the callback lands the moment it is asked for. The contract did not change — the thing on the other end of it did.

Submit the application

- The contract declares this move as `draft → submitted`. From any other state the server refuses it — not from a check somebody wrote for this endpoint, but by reading that line.
- This action also calls `requestTimer` with a `fireAfter` of 72 hours, which emits `platform.timer.requested`. The stand-in the developer registered answers it immediately, so `intake.review_reminder` is already in the event log rather than three days away.
- `submittedAt` is annotated with `snap-processing-clock`, which the shared policy registry resolves to 7 CFR § 273.2(g). SNAP application processing standards — 30-day processing clock from date of filing; expedited service within 7 days for qualifying households.
- `200` and `400`, `404`, `409`, `500` are all declared on this operation, and the server worked out which one applied and returned it. A `409` is declared here because the contract anticipates this call being made out of turn.

Close it from the wrong state

- The contract declares this move as `under_review → closed`, and the record is not in that state yet. Nothing checked for this case on purpose — the server reads that line and answers from it, the same line the moves that worked read.
- Every lifecycle in the set is enforced this way, so a state machine nobody implemented is still a state machine no client app can get around.

Open the application

- `openedAt` was null until now. The lifecycle declares `set: openedAt = $now` on this move, so the field is written because the state machine says so — there is no handler here that writes it.

Close the application

- This move emits `intake.application.closed`, which the log a few steps on will have in it. Nothing subscribed to it and nothing called a publisher: the action declares an `emit` and the server does it.

workflows.description: - A ruleset is a contract of named facts. The server evaluates it at its own endpoint and answers with every fact's value and how sure it is, so the client app can see why, not just what.

steps.description:
Evaluate expeditedSnap

- The answer is not one expression but a chain of named facts. The last is `isExpeditedEligible = (isLowIncome && hasLowResources) || isCombinedUnderShelter || isMigrantWithLowResources` — so the server can say which condition carried, not just what it concluded.
- `incomeThreshold` is an input with a default of 150, citing 7 CFR § 273.2(i)(1)(i). It is a number Congress changes, so the contract treats it as one rather than burying it in code.
- `resourceThreshold` is an input with a default of 100, citing 7 CFR § 273.2(i)(1)(i). It is a number Congress changes, so the contract treats it as one rather than burying it in code.
- Every fact comes back as a `state` and a `value` rather than a bare answer. complete means everything it needed was given to it; a fact that fell back to a declared default says placeholder instead, so the client app can tell a real conclusion from a provisional one.

Gather what the interview flags compare against

- A renewal: a household already on SNAP recertifying.
- `previous` is the household as last certified, copied onto the renewal when it opened, so the baseline holds still through the review. `verified` is what the state's wage records and a verified pay stub show. `asOf` is the interview date.
- The `interviewFlagsInputs` composition translates the data model into the ruleset's inputs by alias — `interviewDate as asOf`, `previousHousehold as previous` — so the rules speak their own vocabulary and nothing between them maps by hand.

Evaluate interviewFlags

- `current` is what the household is reporting in the interview, sent by the client app: the client's mother has moved in with Social Security, warehouse hours were cut, there's cash work cleaning offices, rent went up, and the electric bill is in the client's name. Everything else came from the step before.
- One call answers in two groups: `risks`, situations where payment errors are common, and `inconsistencies`, things in this case that don't agree. `risks.householdChangedSincePrevious` is true — the mother is new — and so is `inconsistencies.wagesDifferFromWageRecords`: the wage records show about 1800 a month, and the household reports about 1100.
- Every flag is worked out from data, never a conclusion the client app sent: ages from dates of birth and the interview date, monthly amounts from what's paid and how often.
- `interviewFlags.risks.elderlyOrDisabledWithoutMedicalCosts` carries more than a true or false. Its annotations give the reason, the questions to probe with, the regulation behind it (`snap-elderly-disabled-deductions`) and the sources the situation comes from.

workflows.description: - Every change sends an event, named for its domain, resource and what happened, into one log shared by every domain.

steps.description:
List the events this walkthrough sent

- Every change the client app made emitted one of these, and nothing asked for them. Uploading a document wrote to this log; so did submitting, opening and closing.
- The types are declared as channels in the contract set — `communication.transcript.created`, `communication.transcript.updated`, `communication.transcript.deleted`, `communication.transcript_entry.created`, and the rest.
- One log, every domain. Nothing wired them together.

List the events for the application

- `q` is full text over the whole log, narrowed here to the application the client app created. The document upload drops out — it happened, but to a different subject.
- What is left was written by more than one domain. Submitting the application is what made eligibility start a determination, and neither domain was wired to the other: each declares its own channel, and this log is all they share.
- `sort` works here for the same reason it worked on the applications — this operation declares its own `x-sortable`, over `time`, `type`, `source`. Nothing was written twice to make both endpoints sortable.

workflows.description: - The mock server has a few controls of its own, outside the contracts, for putting its records into a known state.

steps.description:
Empty the store

- No contract declares this endpoint. It belongs to the mock server, not to the system it is running.
- It clears records, never contracts — afterwards the API is exactly the API it was.

Put the data back

- The records come from the contract set's own `*-mock-data.yaml`, and are checked against the same schemas as anything a client app sends.

info.title: A suggestion, from proposal to decision
info.description: A suggestion is a record that proposes something to a person: something to look into, or a change to make. It waits as `proposed` until the person accepts or dismisses it, and expires if nobody does. Here a caseworker interviews Rosa about her household's income. During the interview, the server proposes suggestions about things to ask, and the assistant proposes changes to her application. The caseworker accepts or dismisses each one.

x-actors.name: The caseworker
x-actors.description: Interviews Rosa, and accepts or dismisses suggestions.

x-actors.name: The interview software
x-actors.description: Records the call, turns what's said into lines and saves them to the transcript.

x-actors.name: The assistant
x-actors.description: An AI model that reads the interview's transcript and proposes changes.

x-actors.name: The server
x-actors.description: Runs the contracts. In this demo, that's the mock server. The interview's state machine runs there, and proposes flags about Rosa's incomes when the interview starts and when they change.

workflows.summary: Setup: Rosa's application before the interview
workflows.description:
- Rosa applied for SNAP and reported four incomes: wages, tips, self-employment income and a salary.
- A pay stub on file shows a higher salary than she reported.

steps.description:
Read Rosa's application details

- `applicationDetails` is a composition: one document the server assembles from several records, here the application with its members and incomes, each keyed by its id. It's editable: a client can change it in one request with a JSON Patch (RFC 6902), a list of changes, each an `op` such as `add` or `replace` at a `path` in the document. The assistant does that later.
- Rosa is the only member. Her incomes are weekly wages that change from week to week, weekly tips of 120 paid in cash, monthly self-employment income, and a monthly salary of 1,100.

Schedule Rosa's interview

- An interview's lifecycle is a state machine in the contracts: the states its `status` can have, and the actions that move it between them.
- `status` is `scheduled`, the state the server gives a new interview.

workflows.description: - When the caseworker starts the interview, the server checks Rosa's incomes against rules and proposes suggestions for the caseworker: things to ask about, and a correction where a pay stub disagrees with what she reported.

steps.description:
Start the interview

- The server moves it to `in_progress` and sets `startedAt`.
- `start` is one of the state machine's actions. Besides changing the status, it runs steps, and one calls `suggestFlags`, a procedure: a named list of steps in the contracts that other steps can call.
- `suggestFlags` reads Rosa's incomes and pay stubs through `interviewFlagsInputs`, a composition shaped as the input the `interviewFlags` ruleset expects, and evaluates the ruleset. A ruleset is a contract of named facts, each worked out from the input. Some facts list incomes to flag, and `suggestFlags` proposes a suggestion for each.

List the suggestions the server proposed

- `q` searches by field: `metadata.intake.interviewId:<id>` finds this interview's suggestions. `metadata` holds whatever the proposer needs to find its suggestions again, under its domain's name; `suggestFlags` keeps the interview's id, the flag, and the income's id (`recordId`).
- `total` is 5.
- There are two kinds. An `informing` suggestion points something out about a record, in a `category` the contract set declares, and names the record (`subjectType`, `subjectId`). Accepting it means the caseworker took it up; nothing changes. An `operation` suggestion carries a `call` to an operation; accepting it makes the call.
- These are deterministic: they come from rules applied to Rosa's data, so the same data always gives the same suggestions. The assistant's suggestions, later, come from an AI model reading the transcript. Either can propose either kind: `kind` says what accepting does, not who proposed it.
- Wages: the amount changes from week to week, so they're flagged `earned-income-varies`, an informing suggestion.
- Tips: the amount changes and they're paid in cash, so they get two suggestions, one under `earned-income-varies` and one under `cash-or-self-employment-income`. Each category on a record is a separate suggestion.
- Self-employment income: it's flagged `cash-or-self-employment-income`.
- Salary: Rosa reported 1,100 a month, and a pay stub shows 1,250. This is an operation suggestion whose `call` is `updateApplicationIncome`, setting the amount to 1,250.
- `expiresAt` is when an undecided suggestion expires: one day after `createdAt`, the default, since `suggestFlags` didn't set one.

Start recording the interview

- A transcript is the record of a conversation. Each thing said is saved to it as an entry, a line.
- When the caseworker starts recording, the interview software starts a transcript of the interview.
- `subjectType: interview` and `subjectId`, the interview's id, say which conversation the transcript records.

workflows.description:
- Rosa mentions child support she didn't report, a daughter who works, and tips higher than she reported. The assistant reads the line from the transcript and suggests three changes, each citing the line as evidence.
- A suggestion is `kind: operation`, and its `call` is the change. A change to one record calls that record's own operation. Changes that depend on each other, like a new member and her income, go together in one JSON Patch to the `applicationDetails` editable composition, through its update, `updateApplicationDetails`.
- Proposing saves nothing but the suggestion. The server checks the call as if it were made now, and rejects a suggestion that repeats one or couldn't succeed.

steps.description:
Save what Rosa says about her household

- Rosa says "I get child support, two fifty a month. My oldest, Maria, lives with us and works part time, about 600 a month. And my tips are more like 135 a week."
- The interview software saves the line as an entry in the interview's transcript, and the assistant reads it from there.
- `Idempotency-Key` makes the request safe to retry: if the software loses the response and sends the line again with the same key, the server answers with the entry it already saved instead of saving a second one.

payload.text: I get child support, two fifty a month. My oldest, Maria, lives with us and works part time, about 600 a month. And my tips are more like 135 a week.
payload.speaker: client

steps.description:
Suggest adding the child support

- A `call` is a request written down to be made later: an operation's `operationId`, with the `parameters` and `requestBody` it would send. Here it's a change to one record: `createApplicationIncome`, adding unearned income of 250 a month.
- `evidence` cites Rosa's line: `sourceType: transcript_entry` and the entry's id as `sourceId`. The server adds `links.source`, where the line is read. Evidence doesn't quote the line, so whoever reads it goes through the transcripts API and its access rules.
- `201`, with `status: proposed`. `fingerprint` is a hash of the change, used to detect duplicates.

Suggest adding Maria and her income in one change

- Maria's income names her as its member, so the two go in one patch. The assistant makes up an id for Maria, and the income uses it as its `memberId`, so it points at Maria before she's saved.
- The suggestion cites Rosa's line twice: once with Maria's path in the patch, and once with her income's, to say the line supports both changes. A `path` that matches no change in the patch would get `422`.
- `201`. The server tried the patch on a copy of the application's details, checking each change against its record's own operation.

Suggest correcting Rosa's tips

- The details say 120 a week, and Rosa says 135. The patch first checks that the tips are still 120 (`test`), then changes them to 135 (`replace`). Every `replace` needs a `test` right before it, checking the value the assistant read.
- The evidence's `path` is the changed amount.

Suggest Maria again, under different ids and with no evidence

- `409`: it repeats the open suggestion, which `details` names.
- The fingerprint covers the change, but not the ids made up for new records, and not the evidence. So this has the same fingerprint as the first.

Suggest Maria's income without Maria

- `422`: the income names a member who isn't on the application and isn't added in the same patch. A new member and her income go in one patch.

workflows.description:
- Every request carries who makes it, in `X-Caller-Id`: `worker-1` for the caseworker, `assistant-1` for the assistant. Accepting makes the suggestion's call as the person accepting, so the operation's checks and permissions apply to the caseworker, not the assistant.
- The caseworker can correct values first, but not what the call changes.
- Rosa corrects two amounts, and the caseworker changes the tips by hand, so the assistant's tips correction no longer applies when it's accepted.

steps.description:
Accept the salary correction

- The request has no body, so the proposed call runs unchanged.
- `status` is `accepted`, and `performed` shows the call that ran, setting Rosa's salary to 1,250, the amount on the pay stub.

Dismiss the wages flag with a reason

- The caseworker asked Rosa about her wages, and her pay stubs explain why they change.
- `status` is `dismissed`, and the suggestion keeps the `reason`.

payload.reason: Her pay stubs explain the changes.

steps.description:
Read the line the child support suggestion cites

- The caseworker reads the line at the evidence's `links.source`. The server builds that link from the entry, so it includes the transcript the line is in, and the suggestion alone is enough to find it.

Accept the child support with the amount corrected

- Rosa says it's actually 200 a month, not 250. The caseworker sends the `call` with the amount changed to 200.
- `status` is `accepted`. `performed` is the call that ran, and `call` still holds what the assistant proposed, 250.

Accept Maria with her income corrected

- Rosa says Maria makes 650 a month, not 600. The caseworker changes 600 to 650 in the patch. A correction can change values, but not which records or fields the patch changes: that would be refused with `409`.
- `200`, and `performed` holds the corrected patch.

Change Rosa's tips before deciding on the tips suggestion

- Rosa checks her pay stubs: her tips are 130 a week. The caseworker sets them to 130 by hand, before deciding on the assistant's suggestion.

Accept the tips correction

- `409`: the patch checks for 120, but the tips are now 130, so nothing in the patch was saved.
- The suggestion's `status` is now `refused`, and `details` holds it. A refused suggestion can be accepted again with a corrected call, or dismissed.

Read the application's details again

- The salary is 1,250, the child support is 200, Maria is a member with her income of 650, and the tips are 130.

List the event for accepting Maria

- Every change sends an event to one log shared by every domain, and `authid` is who made the change. The suggestion doesn't store who decided it; this event does. Here it's `worker-1`, the caseworker who accepted, not the assistant who proposed.

List the events accepting Maria caused

- `causationid` is the id of the event that caused this one, here the acceptance. Accepting caused two: Maria created, by `createApplicationMember`, and her income created, by `createApplicationIncome`. Their checks ran and their events were sent, as if the caseworker had added them by hand, and `authid` is `worker-1`.

workflows.summary: The server reacts to Rosa's answers
workflows.description: - When an income changes, the server sends the event `intake.application_income.updated`. While the interview is in progress, its state machine listens for that event and runs `suggestFlags` again. A flag that still applies is proposed again, and a flag that no longer applies expires.

steps.description:
Update Rosa's wages

- Rosa says her wages are closer to 320 a week, and the caseworker sets `amount` to 320. They still change from week to week.

Record that Rosa's side income is a gift

- Rosa explains that the 400 a month is help from her sister, not self-employment, and the caseworker sets `source` to `unearned`.

List the interview's suggestions

- `total` is still 5. After the wages changed, the server proposed the wages flag again, and that was rejected with `409`, because the caseworker dismissed the same suggestion.
- The flag on the side income is `expired`. It isn't self-employment anymore, so the flag no longer applies.

workflows.description: - When the caseworker completes the interview, the server expires the suggestions nobody decided on, and stops reacting to Rosa's income changes for it.

steps.description:
Complete the interview

- The server moves it to `completed` and sets `completedAt`.

Update Rosa's tips after the interview

- Rosa calls to say her tips are about 140 a week, and the caseworker sets `amount` to 140.

List the interview's open suggestions

- `q` limits the list to this interview's suggestions with `status:proposed`.
- `total` is 0. Nobody decided on the two tips flags, so the server expired them when the interview was completed, and the change to the tips afterwards proposed nothing new.

info.title: A transcript, from start to close
info.description:
The interview software records a caseworker's interview from start to close, then starts a second transcript that nobody speaks into, exercising the transcription domain end to end:

- profiles, and what a transcript needs before it can start
- asking how to stream audio to the transcription service, with the developer standing in for the state's transcripts adapter
- a timeline of lines, gaps and pauses, each judged by when it started
- retries recognized by their Idempotency-Key, and entries that never change
- closing, and the idle timeout, with the developer standing in for the scheduler

x-actors.name: The administrator
x-actors.description: Sets up the transcription profiles that transcripts are recorded under.

x-actors.name: The caseworker
x-actors.description: Interviews a client, and starts, pauses, resumes and closes the recording.

x-actors.name: The interview software
x-actors.description: Records the call, turns what's said into lines and saves them to the transcript.

x-actors.name: The server
x-actors.description: Runs the contracts. In this demo, that's the mock server. The transcript's state machine runs there.

x-actors.name: The developer
x-actors.description: Runs the demo or test, and uses the mock server's own routes to set things up, like standing in for a scheduler.

workflows.summary: Start, record, pause, resume and close a transcript, and see what it refuses.

steps.description:
Add a profile

- The administrator sent a `TranscriptionProfileCreate` and got back a `TranscriptionProfile`: the shape the administrator writes, and the shape the server keeps.
- `provider` takes its values from the `transcription-services` registry, through `x-enum-source`. `aws-transcribe` is an entry there; a service no entry names is refused, and a contract set adds one with a registry file of its own.
- `source` is `user` for a profile added through the API, and `system` for the ones the config seeds.
- No `idleTimeout`, so transcripts under this profile never close for being idle.

Start without a model

- Refused with `409` by `modelGivenForTheService`: under a profile whose `provider` is a transcription service, a transcript has to say which `model` produced its lines.
- The refusal is the guard's description, written as a sentence. `profileExists` passed, so only the condition not met is named.
- A guard runs on a plain create because the state machine governs `Transcript` under `resources:`. No action is involved.

Start under a profile that does not exist

- Refused with `409` by `profileExists`: the guard reads the profile `profileId` names, through the machine's context, and there isn't one.
- Both guards run, and each one not met is named. `modelGivenForTheService` passes here, since without a profile there is no service to need a model.

Start the transcript

- `TranscriptCreate` requires `profileId`, `client` and `startedAt`. `model` is required by the guard, not the schema, because a profile whose `provider` is `none` needs none.
- `status` is `recording`. The server sets a new transcript to its initial state.
- `startedAt` is by the interview software's clock, and every time on the transcript's entries is compared on that same clock.

Stand in for the transcripts adapter

- The state's transcripts adapter holds the transcription service's secret and issues the short-lived credential the interview software streams with. The mock can't issue one itself: it answers `POST /issue-connection`, a call rather than a resource, with `501`.
- This stub, on the mock server's own route, answers the next `POST /issue-connection` with what Amazon Transcribe's adapter would: a presigned URL that carries the credential, good for five minutes, and the `metadata` the request sent.

Ask how to stream the audio

- `get-connection` is an action of the transcript's state machine, from `recording`. The interview software says what audio it will send and what it can connect over; the server calls the transcripts adapter with those, and with the profile's `provider` and `languages` and the transcript's `model`.
- The answer is a `StreamConnection`: the action's `response` maps it from what the adapter answered, leaving out the adapter's `metadata`. There is no `accessToken` here, since Amazon Transcribe's credential is in the URL.
- The interview software streams audio straight to the service; it never passes through the server. Asking again issues a fresh credential, which is how the software renews one, and how it reconnects.

Add the first line

- `Idempotency-Key` is declared on this operation, from the shared parameters every domain uses. The server remembers the key with its answer.
- The body is a `TranscriptLineCreate`, one of the kinds `TranscriptEntryCreate` chooses between by `kind`.
- `startedWhileRecording`, `endsAfterItStarts` and `gapOutsidePauses` all passed: the guards the machine puts on every new entry.

payload.text: Can you tell me who lives with you?
payload.speaker: staff

steps.description:
Send it again

- Same `Idempotency-Key`, same body: the server answers with the line it already stored, with the same `id` and `Idempotent-Replayed: true`. No second line is written.
- The same key with a different body would be refused with `422`. A retry is the same request; a new request needs a new key.

payload.text: Can you tell me who lives with you?
payload.speaker: staff

steps.description:
Go off the record

- `pause` is an action of the transcript's state machine, from `recording` to `paused`, guarded by `atAfterStart`.
- Its steps write a `pause` entry with no `endedAt`, and emit `paused`, which resolve names `communication.transcript.paused`.
- `at` is by the interview software's clock too. `AtRequest` declares it, for pausing, resuming and closing alike.

Send a line said just before the pause

- It arrived after the pause, but its `startedAt` is before it, and `startedWhileRecording` judges an entry by when it started. Kept.
- The interview software sends a line once it is finished, so a line still being spoken when the pause came always arrives late.

payload.text: My two kids and my mother.
payload.speaker: client

steps.description:
Send a line said during the pause

- Refused with `409` by `startedWhileRecording`: a pause was open when the line started.
- The server refuses it, not the interview software. Nothing said off the record is kept, even if the interview software keeps sending.

Report a lost stretch overlapping the pause

- Refused with `409` by `gapOutsidePauses`. A gap is time the interview software lost, and the pause already accounts for that stretch.
- `cause` says why the time was lost: `connection` here, one of the values `GapCause` declares.

Ask how to stream during the pause

- Refused with `409`: `get-connection` goes only from `recording`. Off the record, there is nothing to stream, so the server issues no credential and doesn't call the adapter.

Go back on the record

- `resume` goes from `paused` to `recording`, guarded by `atAfterPauseBegan`. Resuming a transcript that's already recording succeeds and changes nothing.
- It gives the open pause its `endedAt` with a `PATCH` the server makes itself, then calls `requestIdleCheck`, which does nothing here: this profile has no `idleTimeout`.

Send a late line from inside the past pause

- Still refused by `startedWhileRecording`: the pause is over, but the line started inside it.

Read the timeline

- A `TranscriptEntryList`: lines, gaps and pauses together, in the order they happened by `startedAt`.
- `total` is 3: the two lines kept, and the pause with the `endedAt` resuming gave it. The refused entries left nothing behind.

Try to change an entry

- Refused with `403`: the machine lets only `system` update a `TranscriptEntry`, and the interview software's role is checked before the body is.
- Resuming and closing end a pause through the machine's own steps, which are not held to this.

Close the transcript

- `close` goes from `recording` or `paused` to `closed`, and sets `closedAt` to the `at` sent.
- `lastActivityAt` is when the last line or gap ended, kept up to date by the machine's subscription to `communication.transcript_entry.created`. A pause doesn't count: it is the transcript's own entry, not the interview software's.

Send a line after the close

- Refused with `409` by `startedWhileRecording`: the line started after `closedAt`.

Add a profile with an idle timeout

- `idleTimeout` is an ISO 8601 duration, `PT30M`. A recording transcript under this profile that hears nothing for that long closes itself.

Stand in for the scheduler

- `requestIdleCheck` emits `platform.timer.requested`, asking the scheduler to send an `idle_check` once the profile's `idleTimeout` has passed.
- Nobody waits 30 minutes in a test. This stub, on the mock server's own route, answers the next idle check request at once, as if the time had passed.

Start a transcript and go quiet

- Creating it asks for the first idle check: the machine's subscription to `communication.transcript.created` calls `requestIdleCheck`.
- No line or gap ever arrives.

Read the quiet transcript

- When the `idle_check` came, nothing had arrived since it was asked for, so the server closed the transcript.
- It closed at `lastActivityAt`, or at `startedAt` when there was none, as here. An idle transcript closes when it was last heard from, not when the check ran.

info.title: A transcription session, from start to close
info.description:
The interview software keeps track of its connection to the transcription service through a session, from start to close. The session runs in the page; its actions call the transcript's operations, so everything kept is the transcript's.

- starting the transcript the first time the software asks how to stream
- lines in progress, which are only shown, and finished lines, which are kept once
- renewing the credential, going off the record, and a dropped connection
- stopping, with the last line arriving after Stop

x-actors.description: Starts, pauses, resumes and stops the session from the page.

x-actors.name: The client adapter
x-actors.description: Streams the audio to the transcription service and tells the session what happens.

x-actors.name: The server
x-actors.description: Runs the contracts. In this demo, that's the mock server, which also stands in for the page.

x-actors.description: Runs the demo or test, and stands in for the state's server adapter with the mock server's own routes.

workflows.summary: Start a session, stream, pause, resume, lose the connection, and stop.

steps.description:
Add a profile

- The transcription service and languages transcripts are started under.

Start a session

- It says what to start a transcript with: the profile, the model, the software and when the conversation began. No transcript exists yet.
- The session begins in `created`.

Send a finished line before connecting

- Refused with `409`: a line is added only while connected, paused or stopping.

Stand in for the server adapter

- The state's server adapter issues the short-lived credential the software streams with. This stub, on the mock server's own route, answers its operation, `POST /issue-connection`, once; each later connection registers another.

Ask how to stream

- The session has no transcript yet, so `get-connection` starts one, under the profile it was created with, then gets where to connect and a credential through the transcript's own `get-connection`.
- The session is `connecting` until the software says the connection is open.

Read the session

- It now names the transcript it started.

Say the connection is open

- The software opened the connection to the service itself; only it knows it worked. The session is `connected`.

Show a line in progress

- Sent as the service revises it, with the line's key. It's only an event, `line_updated`, for the page to show; nothing is kept.

Add the finished line

- The session adds it to the transcript, with the line's key as its `Idempotency-Key`, and sends `line_added` with the key and the new entry, so the page swaps one for the other.

payload.text: Can you tell me who lives with you?
payload.speaker: staff

steps.description:
Send it again

- A retry with the same key: the transcript recognizes it and keeps the line once.

payload.text: Can you tell me who lives with you?
payload.speaker: staff

steps.description: Stand in for the server adapter for the renewal

Renew the credential

- While connected, `renew-connection` gets a fresh credential and leaves the session `connected`; the connection isn't dropped.

Go off the record

- The page pauses the session, which pauses the transcript on the server and sends `paused`; the software closes the connection, so no audio leaves the page.

Read the transcript

- The pause is kept on the transcript, which is `paused` too.

Go back on the record

- The session resumes the transcript and is `connecting`: the software asks how to stream again.
Stand in for the server adapter for the reconnect after the pause

Ask how to stream again

- The session already has its transcript, so it only gets a new credential.
Say the connection is open again

Lose the connection

- The session is `disconnected`, and the software tries again.
Stand in for the server adapter for the reconnect
Ask how to stream after the drop

Say the connection is open, and what was lost

- The stretch nothing was captured in is recorded on the transcript as a gap.

Stop

- The session is `stopping`; the software sends the end of the audio and waits for the last text.

Add the last line, after Stop

- Still added: lines are accepted while stopping, and it began before the transcript closes.

Close

- The last text is in and the connection is closed. The session closes the transcript, at the time the software says.

Read the transcript's timeline

- The first line once, despite the retry; the pause; the gap from the dropped connection; and the last line. Nothing from the line in progress.
